identified_problem: Practical demonstrations are rated Weak on workload: checkoff appointments took about 80% of TA office-hour time and ran over schedule, and oral defences need substantial staff time [R95], [R16], [R04]. They are only Moderate on scalability and feasibility, since cost rises roughly with cohort size [R95], [R80]. They are also Moderate on authorship, process visibility and appropriate AI use, because a demo alone does not show who produced each part or how AI was used unless paired with repository history or AI logs [R81], [R79], [R72], and on equity, because live formats can disadvantage anxious students and those with lower language proficiency [R81], [R04], [S001].
recommended_redesign: Run short, live, rubric-based demonstrations of about 5-15 minutes in booked, time-limited slots, with scripted questions and a request to modify the code on the spot [R95], [R80], [J4].

Place the demo on top of an AI-permitted project with disclosure and verification requirements, and examine repository history and AI logs during the demo rather than treating the demo as sole proof [R80], [R79], [R93], [R81].
Standardise delivery with prepared environments such as Docker containers, several question versions to limit sharing, and pair formats or closed sign-ups to manage queues [R95].
Offer reattempts and quieter spaces, and keep live demos in person or real time, since recorded or scripted walkthroughs are more exposed to AI support [R95], [S001], [R72].
justification: Finding: in a 60-student programming module, live code demonstrations averaged about 43.9% against about 83.8% on take-home work [R81], and live checkoffs let TAs confirm individual baseline proficiency in real tools for 237 students, with 85-93% of respondents saying they improved their skills [R95]. Finding: individual vivas with live code modification separated students within the same group [R80], [R79]. Interpretation: live demonstration is one of the few formats that tests whether students can explain and adapt their own work, so the redesign keeps it but makes it short, scheduled and linked to process evidence to contain staff time and to show how AI was used [R95], [R81].
implementation_considerations: Cohort: demonstrations are well evidenced for small cohorts of about 14-35 [R72], [R79], workable for medium cohorts of about 50-60 with scheduled slots [R93], [R81], and shown feasible for large cohorts only with short timed slots, appointments and many TAs, with queues and overruns reported [R95], [R80].

Staff time: budget TA or tutor time for live slots, since checkoffs took about 80% of TA office-hour time and ran longer than planned (median 9.5, 19 and 25 minutes against 5, 15 and 15) [R95]; no study measured staff hours per student at scale [R80].
Cost: little policy or licence change is needed, and equipment costs can be kept low, as with low-cost ESP32 hardware [R79]; the main cost is staff time and prepared environments [R95].
Scheduling: demand peaked on the last day, so avoid other large deadlines in demo week and use closed sign-ups [R95].

Equity: provide reattempts, quieter spaces and accessible alternatives, and triangulate with other evidence; no study measured outcomes for students with disabilities, anxiety or English as an additional language [R95], [R16], [R81].
evidence_status_basis: Live demonstrations were implemented and reported in computing courses (computing = Y in tested_redesigns.md): live checkoffs with scripted questions, rubrics and two attempts for 237 students, with scores, surveys and queue logs [R95]; a supervised live demo combined with repository history and a viva for 60 students, with descriptive score and integrity-score changes [R81]; and 10-minute vivas with real-time code modification on an AI-permitted project for over 750 students [R80]. Demos combined with prompt logs and checkpoints were also reported in partly computing engineering courses [R79], [R93]. All are descriptive reports without control groups.
risks_and_limits: A demo shows understanding at one point in time; it does not establish who produced each part or how AI was used without companion process evidence [R81], [R79]. No study tested current GenAI against live computing demos, including real-time AI help during remote demos. Checkoff scores showed ceiling effects, so demos confirm baseline proficiency rather than grade it [R95], and inter-rater reliability of demo rubrics was not reported. Logs examined during the demo improve transparency but do not on their own establish understanding [J6], [D26].
